messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Six months ago, the sedan Amir was riding in with his younger brother, Tariq, struck a guardrail at forty miles per hour. Amir’s recollection fractures around the impact itself; there are long, dark stretches where the timeline simply stops. What remains is vividly intact. The passenger door buckled inward, and Tariq lay slumped against the shattered glass, his face pale, a deep laceration mapping his forehead, another wound on his arm weeping through the sleeve. The air inside the cabin was thick with the sharp, chemical tang of antiseptic wipes from the first responder kit Amir instinctively grabbed. When Tariq was rushed to the regional hospital, the corridor was lined with the same sterile scent, and Amir sat on the edge of the waiting room chair, staring at the floor. He remembers the faces of other patients wheeled past, the grimace of a man with a crushed hand, the quiet panic of a woman clutching her ribs. His mind tells him he should have done more. He tells himself he failed to keep Tariq safe, that the crash proved he is no longer the reliable brother he used to be. He feels permanently altered, as if the impact cracked something inside him that cannot be welded back together. Those memories do not stay buried. When they surface, they arrive as a complete sensory assault. The taste of copper, the heat of the engine hood, the sound of glass crunching, the sight of Tariq’s open wounds, it all returns at once, carrying the exact terror he felt in the minutes after the collision. Amir fights it by holding his breath and pushing the images away, but the effort leaves him hollow. He tells himself he cannot trust his own hands to stabilize a patient. The work shifts grow harder to face. Instead of calling out, he overcompensates. He arrives hours early, meticulously restocking trauma bags, running endless diagnostics on the EKG machines, answering non-urgent dispatch codes for colleagues who are already overwhelmed. He throws himself into the paperwork, the equipment checks, the mundane logistics, anything that keeps his hands busy and his mind from drifting. The habit solidifies over weeks. His wife, Layla, notices the distance. When she reaches out to steady him from behind while he is loading supplies, he flinches so sharply he knocks a tray of bandages to the floor. He reacts with immediate alarm to any unexpected touch, his pulse hammering in his throat. He stops taking public transit, always mapping his commute to ensure he can sit near an exit or in the back corner where he feels shielded. At work, the antiseptic scent of the station supply closet triggers a sudden tightness in his chest. He avoids the trauma bay when possible, his eyes darting to the visible wounds on patients before he can force himself to look away. His supervisors note the gaps in his documentation and the way his focus fragments during radio checks. He tries to concentrate, but the noise of the bay and the sight of bleeding patients pull his attention inward. He tells himself he cannot rely on himself to make split-second decisions when his own mind is racing toward the crash site. The turning point came when the shift commander finally asked him to take a medical leave, citing the risk of compromised patient care during his most vulnerable moments. Amir agreed, but the silence at home has only magnified the fear. He sits on the edge of the sofa, shoulders tense, scanning the doorway of their kitchen. He has come to believe he is fundamentally broken, that the brother he used to be is gone, and that he will always be too fractured to carry a stretcher or trust his own judgment. He is seeking help not because the panic has stopped, but because he is terrified of what he might do if he keeps trying to outrun it. He hopes, perhaps, to find a way to sit in the same room as his brother without bracing for the crash, to work without needing to exhaust himself first, and to stop feeling like a man permanently stranded at the edge of a guardrail.
